area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly and explain a stabilized short-field approach at the recommended speed ±5 knots, touch down within 100 feet of a chosen point and stop with the manufacturer's braking technique, work a landing distance chart with a learner, and spot, explain and fix the short-field errors learners make most.
why: The landing phase causes more pilot-caused accidents than any other single phase of flight, and the most critical landings combine high weight, high density altitude and unfavorable wind [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. A short-field landing leaves almost no margin: it is flown close to the stall [[24:193|AFH 9-22]], and the AIH warns instructors that this slow approach speed reduces safety margins [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Your learner's first real short strip will go the way you trained it.

warmup: Think first: your learner flies a beautiful short-field approach, right on speed, and touches down 250 feet past the point you chose. On a long runway nobody would notice. Where in the approach did those 250 feet come from, and how would you find out before you say a word about it?

key_terms.def: A low-speed, power-on approach used at fields with a short landing area or with obstacles that limit it, closely related to flight near minimum controllable airspeed [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
The spot a constant-angle glide path points at. It does not move in the windshield. It is not the touchdown point, because the round out carries the airplane farther [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point at a constant final descent airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
The stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration; with no published speed the short-field approach uses not more than 1.3 VSO [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

How much the gusts exceed the steady wind; the sources do not define it, and this lesson takes 8 gusting 16 as an 8-knot gust factor. In gusty air no more than one-half of it is added to the short-field approach speed [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
A nose-high, power-assisted descent used to clear obstacles on the way to a short runway, normally no faster than 1.3 VSO, with a steeper than normal angle [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
Holding the positive pitch attitude after touchdown, while the elevator is still effective and if the manufacturer recommends it, so drag helps slow the airplane [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Brake pressure just short of locking the wheels: they still turn, but with great reluctance. It gives the best braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
An AC 91-79B multiplier applied to the unfactored AFM/POH landing distance for the runway condition; the factors include a 15 percent safety margin [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].
Tires riding on a thin sheet of water instead of the runway, so braking and directional control are almost nil [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
Landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, an intersecting taxiway or another designated point on the runway [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]].
The runway distance available for a LAHSO landing, published in the Chart Supplement and the Terminal Procedures Publication [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

chunks.title: Purpose, procedure and the standard you hold

body.p: Purpose: the short-field approach and landing is for a field with a relatively short landing area, or where obstacles on the approach limit the landing area [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. The pilot needs precise, positive control of sink rate and airspeed, an approach that clears any obstacle, little or no float, and a stop in the shortest possible distance [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. It builds on the normal approach and landing; the flare, crosswind and go-around basics are in the Normal Approach and Landing lesson (AI.VII.B). This lesson covers what is different.

Procedures: use the AFM/POH short-field procedure [[24:192|AFH 9-21]], because the manufacturer's procedures and speeds take precedence over any handbook [[24:172|AFH 9-1]]. The AFH's general version:

bullets: When safety and conditions permit, fly a wider pattern with a longer final, so there is time to settle the descent angle after configuring and trimming [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Start the final at least 500 feet above the touchdown area [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

In many airplanes, fly the stabilized final with the flap setting before full flaps. When the field is made, extend full flaps and lower the nose to hold airspeed and keep the aiming point still in the windshield [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Over the obstacle, power may come back slightly; ideally the power then comes off slowly [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Touch down at minimum controllable airspeed, close to the power-off stall attitude [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Hold the nose up for aerodynamic braking if the manufacturer recommends it, then apply maximum braking as soon as the nosewheel is down [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

callout.text: ACS AI.VII.F.S7: “Maintain manufacturer’s published approach airspeed or in its absence not more than 1.3 times the stalling speed or the minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration (VSO), ±5 knots with gust factor applied.” ACS AI.VII.F.S10: “Touch down at a proper pitch attitude within 100 feet beyond or on the specified point, threshold markings, or runway numbers, with no side drift, minimum float, and with the airplane’s longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway centerline.”

body.p: The commercial ACS uses the same ±5 knots and 100 feet (ACS CA.IV.F.S7, S10). Your extra burden is hitting them while you talk. S11 asks for the manufacturer's configuration and braking, so know your POH short-field page cold before the checkride.

check.q: Your private learner touches down 160 feet past the chosen point at the right speed. How does that grade on the private ride, and on yours?
check.a: Inside the private 200-foot window (ACS PA.IV.F.S10), but outside the 100-foot window on the CFI ride (ACS AI.VII.F.S10).

chunks.title: Steep, stabilized and slow: energy on a short final

body.p: A stabilized approach is essential on a short field [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. It is a constant-angle path to a chosen point at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Once on final, the pilot changes power and pitch together to set the descent angle and airspeed, then makes only small changes to correct [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

Energy management concepts: the throttle controls total energy, and the elevator only shares it out between altitude and airspeed. Neither control sets altitude or airspeed alone [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. On a short final that means:

Correction from the AFH

Reduce power while lowering the pitch to steepen the path and raise the sink rate [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]

Add power while raising the pitch to shallow the path and cut the sink rate [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]

Raising the nose here increases the sink rate. Add power early; if too slow and too low, go around [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]

body.p: Why the short field is special: this approach is flown at a steep angle close to the stall [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. The AFH calls it a minimum safe airspeed descent, where too much sink or 'mushing' can take a lot of power to stop [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. At the slow edge of the envelope, an unstable or slow approach can produce a sink rate that even full power cannot reverse. Then the only fix is to lower the nose first, and near the ground there may be no room [[24:99|AFH 4-13]] [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

callout.text: The AFH stabilized criteria call for a go-around if not stabilized by 500 feet above airport elevation in VMC, and an immediate go-around if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL in a typical GA pattern [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. On a short field, a late fix to a bad approach usually costs more runway than it saves (S12).

Spot slides down in the windshield: you will land beyond it, so steepen. Spot rises toward the horizon: you will land short, so shallow [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Power and pitch move together on a short final.

check.q: Slow and nose high on a short final, your learner raises the nose a little more to 'stretch' to the point. What does that do, and what is your coaching line?
check.a: At high angle of attack and low speed, more pitch increases the sink rate [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Say: 'Power up, hold the attitude,' and go around if it is too slow and too low [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

chunks.title: Approach speed: what 'on speed' means here

bullets: Use the manufacturer's recommended speed. With none published, fly not more than 1.3 VSO [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
In gusty air, add no more than one-half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
The AFM/POH landing speeds are generally the minimum safe speeds. Slower can mean a stall, poor control or a high sink rate [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
A 10 percent excess landing speed causes at least a 21 percent increase in landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. AC 91-79B uses 20 percent as a rule of thumb [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].
A heavier airplane needs more speed: a 21 percent increase in landing weight needs a 10 percent increase in landing speed [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Some POHs give the speed by weight.

body.p: Too fast is the classic short-field killer: extra speed can put the touchdown too far from the threshold or make the roll longer than the landing area [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Too slow is the other one: the learner cannot flare and lands hard (AFH error 4) [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

The proof of the right speed shows at the end: little or no float in the flare, with enough control to touch down properly, verifies the approach speed was correct [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Teach the learner to judge the approach by the flare, not only by the needle.

callout.text: Sources differ on the window. The AFH stabilized criteria allow +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Your CFI standard is ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.F.S7). Fly and teach ±5; on a short runway the 'plus 10' is runway you do not have.

Instructional risk: on short-field landings some airplanes fly a slower approach speed, and the instructor must stay alert to anything that cuts safety margins [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Guard the throttle and the yoke on every slow final.

check.q: Your learner says, 'It's bumpy, so I'll carry 10 extra knots on this short runway.' The POH speed is 60 knots. What does that cost?
check.a: 10 knots is about 17 percent fast, and a 10 percent excess alone costs at least 21 percent more landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Add no more than half the gust factor instead [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

chunks.title: Aim point, touchdown point and the 100-foot box

body.p: The short-field landing is an accuracy approach to an aiming point [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. The aiming point is not where the wheels touch: the round out carries the airplane farther, and with float the pilot can predict the touchdown with some accuracy [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. With a correct short-field speed, float is small, so the gap between aim and touchdown is small too.
Select the touchdown point considering the wind conditions, landing surface, and obstructions:

bullets: Obstructions: with obstacles present, a slightly steeper approach angle puts the touchdown closer to the obstacle and leaves more room to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

Wind conditions: wind changes the glide distance over the ground, and the pilot corrects for it with pitch and power [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]; a tailwind also raises the touchdown groundspeed and the landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
Landing surface: choose a point that leaves room to stop on the surface you have; wet, grass or downhill surfaces need more [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

Teach the choice, do not hand it over: the AIH says aiming and touchdown points should not be picked mechanically. The instructor teaches how to choose them from the airplane, the landing type, the conditions and the expected performance [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

body.p: Floating is the 100-foot window's enemy. Extra speed usually causes it, and the airplane can be well past the point before touchdown. Prolonged floating should be avoided, especially on short runways [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. AC 91-79B adds that a long touchdown may make the calculated landing distance impossible to achieve [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]], and that achieving the intended touchdown point comes first, because wheel brakes slow the airplane far better than air drag [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.8.1]].

How big is 100 feet? Standard centerline stripes are 120 feet long with 80-foot gaps [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]], so the window is less than one stripe. Some runways shorten stripes and gaps to fit [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]], so check before you grade against them.

callout.text: Grade every practice landing out loud: 'Point was the second stripe; we touched 40 feet past.' Feedback the learner can measure beats 'nice landing.' Vary the point from landing to landing, too: the AIH suggests varying a maneuver to check that a learner understands the principle, not just the routine [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: Why does the aiming point have to sit a little short of where you want the wheels?
check.a: The round out reduces the sink rate, so the actual touchdown happens farther down the runway than the aiming point [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

chunks.title: Simulating an obstacle with a learner

body.p: Real short strips with trees are not where you start. What the sources do give you to build a simulated obstacle:

bullets: POH landing charts give a total distance to clear a 50-foot obstacle as well as the ground roll [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].
AFM landing distances assume the airplane crosses the threshold at 50 feet; every 10 feet higher adds about 200 feet of landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].
Obstacles call for a slightly steeper approach so the touchdown comes closer to the obstacle [[24:192|AFH 9-21]], flown as a minimum safe airspeed descent [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

Over the obstacle, power comes back only slightly and then slowly; closing the throttle too rapidly can bring an immediate increase in sink rate and a hard landing [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

body.p: For takeoffs, the AIH says the instructor can specify where an imaginary obstacle exists, at a realistic point [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Application (no source gives a landing method): do the same for landings and brief the obstacle on the ground. For example, 'a 50-foot tree line at the threshold, and our point is the second stripe.' In the air, call it once on final, then grade two things: did the path stay above an imaginary 50 feet at the threshold, and did the wheels land within 100 feet of the point? The AIH's phase II idea fits here: discuss on the ground what a 1,800-foot strip with an obstruction off the departure end would mean for this airplane, even though you train on a long runway [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

Scan the landing runway and adjoining area for traffic and obstructions: make the learner clear the approach path, the runway and the areas beside it on every final, real obstacle or not. Pilots should verify the landing surface on every final [[24:175|AFH 9-4]], and a vehicle or animal on a short runway is an obstruction you cannot fly around.

callout.text: Never make a real obstacle the training aid by dragging in low over it. A long, low, high-power final close to the ground is the wrong way to fix a low approach [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. Keep the simulated obstacle imaginary, and keep the path at or above it.

check.q: Your learner crosses the threshold at 80 feet instead of the 50 the chart assumes. About how much landing distance does that add?
check.a: About 600 feet: 200 feet for each 10 feet above 50, and 30 / 10 x 200 = 600 [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

chunks.title: Round out, touchdown and maximum braking

body.p: The flare needs accurate timing: from a steep, slow approach, start too late and you fly into the ground; too early and you stall high and sink fast [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Touch down at minimum controllable airspeed in about the power-off stall attitude [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

bullets: Power: do not close the throttle too fast; it can bring an immediate increase in sink rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
A little power keeps airflow over the elevator for the flare; at low speed a windmilling propeller can block that airflow and make the flare hard [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
After touchdown: hold the positive pitch attitude while the elevator works, if the manufacturer recommends it, for aerodynamic braking [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Nosewheel down: apply maximum braking at once to keep the roll short [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Hold the yoke full back while braking smoothly; the airplane leans forward under heavy braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Best braking is an incipient skid. A locked wheel skids, braking drops dramatically and tires can be damaged [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

body.p: For most airplanes, aerodynamic drag does most of the slowing in the first quarter of the speed decay, and brakes get better as airspeed and lift fall away [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. If the approach speed was right and the touchdown was at minimum speed, excessive braking should not be needed [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

Configuration: some manufacturers recommend flap retraction on the rollout of a short-field landing to improve braking. Then the pilot must positively identify the flap handle first; pilots have retracted the gear instead of the flaps [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Follow the POH (ACS AI.VII.F.S11).

callout.text: Make sure the learner's feet are off the brakes at touchdown. Early braking can drop the nose suddenly and lose the aerodynamic braking [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

check.q: Your learner stands on the brakes and you hear the tires chirp and skid. What is the coaching line?
check.a: Ease off to just short of lock-up, an incipient skid, with the yoke full back. A locked wheel brakes much less and can damage the tire [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

chunks.title: Landing distance with a learner: the chart

callout.text: Before every flight the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data from the approved flight manual, or other reliable data for elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Work one chart together on the ground. In the 172R table, read the conditions box before any number: flaps 30°, power off, maximum braking, paved, level, dry runway, zero wind, 62 KIAS at 50 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. Then the notes: subtract 10 percent per 9 knots of headwind; add 10 percent per 2 knots of tailwind up to 10 knots; on dry grass add 45 percent of the ground roll figure; flaps up means 7 knots faster and 35 percent longer [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

Worked example: 2,000 feet pressure altitude and 20 °C gives a 605-foot ground roll and 1,375 feet over a 50-foot obstacle [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. Point out that the ground roll is less than half the total: the air distance from 50 feet is most of the job, which is why speed and the touchdown point matter so much.

Then teach what the number assumes. Chart data come from a new airplane flown with average piloting skill, in good working order [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. The 172R number needs maximum braking and the POH technique [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. A dragged-in, fast or floating approach will not produce it.
Selection of runway based on pilot capability, airplane performance and limitations, available distance, and wind:

bullets: Available distance: takeoff and landing get more hazardous as the computed performance approaches the runway length [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

Pilot capability: the RMH sample shows a single-engine pilot whose shortest comfortable runway is 2,500 feet [[30:16|RMH 2-4]], and suggests at least 500 more feet at an unfamiliar airport [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

Margins: AC 91-79B factors for a reciprocating airplane start at 1.67 times the dry, unfactored book distance and rise as braking gets worse; they include a 15 percent safety margin [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].
Wind: land into the wind when you can. A tailwind adds about 21 percent for 10 knots [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]], and on a contaminated runway crosswind can limit braking [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.10]].

callout.text: Teaching tip: have the learner work the numbers first and tell you the answer, then ask, 'Would you land there with your skill today?' That makes the chart a decision tool, not homework. Personal minimums are not changed to make a flight happen [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: From the 172R chart, what total distance over a 50-foot obstacle does the table give at 6,000 feet and 30 °C?
check.a: 1,565 feet, with a 725-foot ground roll [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

chunks.title: Air, weight, tailwind and the landing surface

body.p: Effects of atmospheric conditions: at altitude the airplane lands at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed, so it needs more distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. The minimum landing distance at 5,000 feet is 16 percent greater than at sea level, about 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Weight matters too: 10 percent heavier means about 5 percent faster and 10 percent longer [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

Tailwind: the airplane lands at the same airspeed, so a tailwind raises the touchdown groundspeed. A 10-knot tailwind adds about 21 percent [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]] [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. Some small-airplane charts are harsher: the Cessna 150 and 152 note adds 10 percent for each 2 knots [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.9.1]]. A slippery runway plus a tailwind is especially risky because of the higher groundspeed and the chance of floating [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]].

body.p: Hydroplaning starts at about 9 times the square root of the tire pressure, and once started it can continue well below that speed. Landing faster than recommended raises the risk [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. On a wet runway, land into the wind, avoid abrupt control inputs and use aerodynamic braking fully [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

callout.text: Teaching point: the most critical landings combine high weight, high density altitude and unfavorable wind [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Build one ground scenario that stacks all three on a short, wet runway and let the learner find the 'no' on their own.

check.q: Main tires at 25 psi. At about what speed can dynamic hydroplaning begin?
check.a: 9 x square root of 25 = 9 x 5 = 45 knots [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

body.p: Wind correction techniques on approach and landing are the same as for any crosswind landing (see AI.VII.B): the crab method, or the wing-low (sideslip) method, which the AFH recommends in most cases, while pilots should learn both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. On a long final, one option is to crab first and change to wing-low before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
Crosswind: what changes on a short field:

bullets: Full flaps and crosswind: the upwind wing's flap catches more wind. Near the ground, wind on the deflected flap tends to yaw the airplane into the wind and raise the upwind wing; aileron into the wind is essential, and it may be necessary to retract flaps soon after touchdown [[24:235|AFH 12-4]].

Less control at low speed: as the airplane slows in the flare, controls get less effective and the correction must grow [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. A short-field flare is slower than a normal one, so expect bigger inputs.

Rollout: keep adding aileron into the wind as the airplane slows, full aileron as it stops [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]. Heavy braking is not a steering tool; roll-over can be avoided with aileron, rudder or the steerable nosewheel, but not brakes [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

Limits: airplanes are shown controllable in 90° crosswinds up to 0.2 VSO [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn in a slip, the wind is too strong for that runway [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

body.p: Maintain directional control and crosswind correction all the way: touch down with no drift and the axis aligned with the centerline (ACS AI.VII.F.S10). Touching down while drifting and excessive braking are both on the AFH crosswind error list [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

callout.text: Teaching order: add crosswind to the short-field landing only after the learner can do each one well alone. The AIH lists unexpected crosswinds among the challenges a learner masters individually before combining them [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

check.q: With full flaps in a stiff crosswind, why might the airplane try to turn into the wind right after touchdown?
check.a: Wind striking the deflected flap behind the main gear yaws the airplane into the wind and raises the upwind wing; hold aileron into the wind, and the flaps may need to come up [[24:235|AFH 12-4]].

chunks.title: Windshear and wake turbulence on a short final

body.p: Windshear: a headwind turning into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance. A microburst encounter on approach brings the same sequence as on takeoff and can force the airplane to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A short-field approach starts close to the stall, so there is little airspeed to give away.

In the AWH approach case, the airplane met an increasing downdraft and tailwind, lost airspeed, dropped below the glidepath and hit short of the threshold. The natural nose-down response to low airspeed added altitude loss, and pitch and recovery came too late [[28:271|AWH 22-16]] [[28:272|AWH 22-17]]. The AWH says a stabilized approach with clear callouts is essential to spot a bad trend [[28:272|AWH 22-17]], and to watch for microburst signs early and be ready to go around at the first sign [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].
Wake turbulence: the AIM landing procedures matter more on a short runway, because some of them push your touchdown point:

Stay at or above its path, note its touchdown point, land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
If 'beyond it' leaves too little runway, wait or use another runway (application); the pilot is ultimately responsible for an appropriate interval [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]

Usually fits a short-field touchdown

body.p: A light crosswind of 1 to 5 knots can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone, and a tailwind can move vortices forward into it; the light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Whether or not ATC warns you, you are expected to adjust your flight path to avoid serious wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

callout.text: Teach the learner that a short runway behind a larger airplane is often a 'not now' decision. The AIM procedure and the short-field touchdown can conflict, and the AIM gives no exception.

check.q: A larger airplane just made a touch-and-go on your short runway in a light quartering wind. When can your learner land?
check.a: After at least 2 minutes, because vortices settle and drift along the runway [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

body.p: Rejected landing and go-around: a go-around is a normal maneuver, and an aborted landing is not proof of poor skill [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. It becomes dangerous only when delayed or done wrong. The usual causes of delay are landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. On a short field, brief a go-around trigger before every approach: not stabilized by the gate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], a touchdown that will not happen near the point, or a float past it. Failure to recognize and abort a poor approach is on the AFH short-field error list [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

bullets: Power first: full power smoothly, without hesitation [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Attitude: the airplane is trimmed for slow flight and full power raises the nose and yaws left. Expect strong forward pressure, and resist pitching up without airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Configuration: flaps up in small steps after the descent stops; a sudden full retraction can settle the airplane [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. In a full-flap, nose-up trim go-around, be ready for big pitch force changes [[24:235|AFH 12-4]].
Ground effect: do not climb out of it too early; that 'cushion' is borrowed performance [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: Land and hold short operations (LAHSO): the PIC may accept only after deciding the airplane can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance, and student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Good decision making means knowing beforehand whether you can accept [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. A LAHSO clearance does not preclude a rejected landing; if you go around, keep separation and tell ATC promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

callout.text: Make your learner's go-around call a reflex: decide at a fixed point on short final, out loud. The AIH wants instructors to teach a go-around whenever the landing will not happen in the first third of the runway [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]; on a short field that point comes much earlier.

check.q: After accepting LAHSO, your learner is at taxi speed well before the hold-short point, with a taxiway ahead. What does the AIM expect?
check.a: Exit at the first convenient taxiway before the hold-short point, unless told otherwise [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

chunks.title: Checklists, radios, the right runway, traffic and distraction

bullets: Checklists: finish briefings and checklists before the approach, except the landing checklist, so attention goes to the approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Add a short-field brief: speed, flap plan, aiming point, go-around point.
Radios: at a nontowered field report downwind, base and final, and leaving the runway, with the airport name at both ends [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].
Correct runway: verify alignment and runway number on every final; unfamiliarity, complacency or fatigue cause wrong surface landings. If in doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Scan: the runway and the area around it for traffic and obstructions on every final (chunk 5).

body.p: Collision hazards: in one study of midair collisions, a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the accidents, and most happened in good VFR daylight near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. A wider pattern with a long final, as the AFH suggests for short fields [[24:192|AFH 9-21]], puts you farther from where others expect you. Say your position clearly.

Low altitude maneuvering, including stall, spin, or CFIT: sixty percent of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing, usually when attention was diverted [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. A slow, steep, high-drag final is exactly where that happens. Using pitch alone to stretch the approach leads to a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. CFIT often follows flying too low, at night or in low visibility [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]; a dragged-in final over unseen terrain is a CFIT setup.

Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness, or disorientation: when overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. The instructor is a distraction too: lots of coaching on final can make you miss radio calls and traffic, so use only concise prompting on approach [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

callout.text: Instructor trap: a short-field demo while talking is high workload for you. The AIH warns that conveying information while also checking that the airplane is flown safely can cut your own collision avoidance and situational awareness [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Script your patter so it costs you nothing.

check.q: Why does the AIH want you to cut back to concise prompts on final, even on a training landing?
check.a: Heavy coaching on final can cause missed calls from ATC or pattern traffic and weakens collision avoidance [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

body.p: Building blocks: a learner should master the normal landing before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. Slow flight practice transfers positively to short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]], so fly some slow flight at altitude in landing configuration first. Tie the lesson to both certification and safety [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

head: AIH phase
In the short-field lesson
rows: Phase I: stick and rudder
Power and airspeed management, configuration, pattern placement, wind correction, aim point and sight picture, by repetition [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
Phase II: the factors
Runway conditions, no-flap landings, obstructions and rejected landings, discussed on the ground at little cost [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
Phase III: the scenario
A full flight: a diversion to a short runway, perhaps with a failed flap, where the learner decides whether to land or go elsewhere [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]

body.p: On the ground brief: the POH procedure and speed, the chart numbers for today, the aiming point and simulated obstacle, the stabilized gate and the go-around trigger. In the air: demonstrate while explaining, then let the learner fly to a long runway with a generous point, then tighten the point and add the obstacle. Keep prompts short on final [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
Your patter for the demo (S13 also asks you to analyze errors, see the next chunk):

head: Where
What you say
rows: Downwind
'Wider pattern today. Speed is 62, aim point is the second stripe.'
Final, field made
'Full flaps, nose down a touch, spot stays still in the windshield.'
Over the threshold
'Power coming off slowly, not all at once.'
Flare
'Small flare, little float. If it floats, we go around.'
Rollout
'Nose held off while it works, nosewheel down, max braking, yoke full back.'

body.p: Let mistakes run only as far as safety allows. The AIH says it is often better to let a learner go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], but a slow, steep final near the ground leaves little room; set your own limit for when you take the controls and say 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: Learners can understand not to trade a stable approach for accuracy and still not be ready to apply it [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Praise the go-around from a floated short-field landing as loudly as a perfect one.

check.q: In the AIH's three-phase plan for short-field landings, where do no-flap landings and rejected landings come in?
check.a: Phase II, the factors that affect the landing, which can be discussed in the ground portion at little extra cost [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

body.p: The errors come from the AFH short-field list [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. The 'what you see' and 'fix' columns use the AFH text around them.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Final that needs an overly steep approach and high sink rate
Base too close or too high; a dive at the spot
Plan the final from at least 500 feet above the touchdown area; avoid diving, since 800 to 1,000 fpm is excessive [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Unstable approach
Speed and path wander; big late corrections
Configure and trim early on a longer final; go around if not stable at the gate [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Undue delay in glide path corrections
Aim point drifting for a while before anything changes
Correct early and small, with power and pitch together [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Too low an airspeed on final
Can't flare properly; hard landing
Power early to restore speed; too slow and too low means go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Too high an airspeed
Long float in the round out
Fly the POH speed; if the float takes you past the point, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Prematurely reducing power to idle on round out
Sudden sink and a hard arrival
Bring the power off slowly; a little power keeps elevator authority [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]
Touchdown with excessive airspeed
Flat, fast touchdown; skipping
Hold off to minimum controllable airspeed in the power-off stall attitude [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]
Excessive and/or unnecessary braking
Chirping or locked tires; nose pitching down
Incipient skid with the yoke full back; with a good approach, heavy braking should not be needed [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Failure to maintain directional control
Swerve on the rollout, especially while braking
Rudder and aileron into the wind; do not steer with heavy braking [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]
Failure to recognize and abort a poor approach
Pressing on when high, fast or floating
Brief a go-around point; go around when in doubt [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]

body.p: On the checkride, the examiner may fly a simulated error. Name it, give the likely cause, say or show the fix, and let the 'learner' try again. Use the AIH idea that judging the learner's mastery of each element counts more than the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: Your learner closes the throttle completely the moment the simulated obstacle is behind them, and the airplane drops hard. Which listed error is that, and what is your fix?
check.a: Prematurely reducing power, which brings a sudden sink and a hard landing. Bring the power off slowly in the round out [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

scenario.title: A short, wet runway on a dual cross-country
scenario.setup: You are instructing a student pilot on a dual cross-country in a 172R at 2,450 pounds. The planned stop is a towered airport at 1,000 feet elevation, 30 °C. Runway 27 is 2,800 feet with trees off the approach end; runway 36 is 4,500 feet. A shower just passed; both runways are smooth (not grooved) and wet, with no standing water reported. Wind is 300 at 8 gusting 16. A larger twin is ahead of you on final for runway 27. The student has flown short-field landings only on your home field's long runway.

questions.q: The student asks for runway 27 'to practice a real short field.' What do the numbers say?
questions.a: The chart gives 1,375 feet over 50 feet at 1,000 feet and 30 °C [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. A wet runway with no standing water is runway condition code 5 [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.6.1]], and the reciprocating factor for a smooth code 5 runway is 2.6: 1,375 x 2.6 = 3,575 feet, more than 2,800 [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. Dry it would be 1,375 x 1.67 = 2,296 feet. Today, take runway 36.

questions.q: What approach speed and touchdown standard do you brief for the student?
questions.a: The POH short-field speed (this chart's 62 KIAS at 50 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]), plus no more than half the 8-knot gust factor, about 4 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Your own standard is ±5 knots and within 100 feet of the point (ACS AI.VII.F.S7, S10).

questions.q: Tower says 'Caution wake turbulence' for the twin landing ahead on 27. If you had kept 27, what would the AIM have you do, and why is that a problem here?
questions.a: Stay at or above its path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. On a short, wet runway that may leave too little room to stop, so wait for a different runway or more time (application).

questions.q: The tower offers 'Runway 36, hold short of runway 27.' Who decides, and what do you answer?
questions.a: The PIC has final authority to accept or decline, and student pilots or pilots unfamiliar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. With a student flying, decline and ask for full length, ideally before the clearance is issued [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

questions.q: On a 1-mile final, airspeed drops 10 knots and the sink rate rises near the shower's edge. What do you expect and do?
questions.a: Possible windshear: a downdraft and tailwind can push the airplane below the path and short of the runway [[28:271|AWH 22-16]]. Go around at the first sign; do not let the student lower the nose to chase airspeed [[28:266|AWH 22-11]] [[28:272|AWH 22-17]].

questions.q: On the next approach the student floats past the aiming point on the wet runway. What now?
questions.a: Go around. Prolonged floating uses runway and should be avoided on short runways [[24:203|AFH 9-32]], wet pavement brings hydroplaning and poor braking [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]], and a long touchdown may make the chart distance unreachable [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist and a short-field brief (speed, flaps, aiming point, go-around point) while explaining why it is done before the approach.
skills.practice: Say the brief on downwind every time; finish everything but the landing checklist before the approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Make the pattern radio calls, towered or nontowered, and explain the phraseology.
skills.practice: Script downwind, base, final and clear-of-runway calls with the airport name at both ends [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].

skills.do: Confirm alignment with the correct or assigned runway on final and explain how wrong surface landings happen.
skills.practice: Check runway number and alignment out loud on every final; go around when in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Scan the landing runway and adjoining area for traffic and obstructions, and point them out as you teach.
skills.practice: Clear final, the runway and its sides on every approach, and call each item you see [[24:175|AFH 9-4]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

skills.do: Select and aim for a touchdown point that suits the wind, surface and obstructions, and explain why that point.
skills.practice: Pick a different point each landing and explain the choice; aim slightly short of it [[24:176|AFH 9-5]] [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

skills.do: Set up the recommended configuration, airspeed and trim, and keep the approach stabilized with pitch and power together.
skills.practice: Fly the flap setting before full flaps until the field is made, then full flaps and lower the nose [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

skills.do: Hold the manufacturer's published approach airspeed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, ±5 knots with gust factor applied, while explaining it (ACS AI.VII.F.S7).
skills.practice: Practice the patter until it costs no airspeed; in gusts add no more than half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and crosswind correction through approach, touchdown and a braking rollout.
skills.practice: Wing-low through the flare, aileron into the wind on the rollout, never steer with brakes [[24:188|AFH 9-17]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

skills.do: Make smooth, timely control inputs before, during and after touchdown, including a gradual power reduction.
skills.practice: Bring the power off slowly in the round out and hold the nose up while it works [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

skills.do: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude within 100 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift, minimum float, aligned with and over the centerline (ACS AI.VII.F.S10).
skills.practice: Grade every landing against a centerline stripe: 120 feet long, 80-foot gaps on standard markings [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]].

skills.do: Use the manufacturer's configuration and braking procedure and explain it, including any flap retraction on the rollout.
skills.practice: Rehearse the POH short-field page; brake to an incipient skid with the yoke full back [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

skills.do: Go around promptly when the approach cannot meet the standards or becomes unsafe, and explain the trigger.
skills.practice: Brief a go-around point each time and fly some go-arounds from full flaps at slow speed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common short-field errors, usually a simulated error flown by the examiner as your 'learner'.
skills.practice: For each error in the table, practice saying what you see, the cause and the fix [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: Your private learner touches down 150 feet past the chosen point. Which statement is correct?
options: It meets neither the private nor the CFI touchdown standard
It meets the CFI standard but not the private standard
It meets both the private and the CFI touchdown standards
It meets the private standard but not the CFI standard
quiz.why: Private allows within 200 feet beyond the point (ACS PA.IV.F.S10); the CFI standard is within 100 feet (ACS AI.VII.F.S10).

quiz.q: For many GA airplanes, which flap setting does the AFH suggest for the stabilized short-field final before the field is made?
options: Flaps up until short final, then full flaps
Whatever setting gives the slowest approach speed
Full flaps from the base turn on
The setting just before full flaps
quiz.why: Many GA airplanes fly the stabilized final with the setting that precedes full flaps, then extend full flaps when the field is made [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

quiz.q: For most airplanes, what does most of the slowing in the first quarter of the speed decay after a short-field touchdown?
options: Wheel brakes at an incipient skid
Rolling friction of the tires
Aerodynamic drag
Retracting the flaps
quiz.why: Aerodynamic drag is the single biggest factor early; brakes become more effective as airspeed and lift decrease [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH want the yoke held full back during maximum braking?
options: Because the airplane tends to lean forward under heavy braking
To keep the nosewheel off the runway for the whole landing roll
To keep lift on the wings for better brake cooling
So the stall horn sounds as a reminder to brake
quiz.why: Back pressure increases braking effectiveness because the airplane tends to lean forward with heavy braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH, practice of which skill gives positive transfer to short-field landings?
options: Steep turns
Turns around a point
Slow flight
Emergency descents
quiz.why: The AIH example: slow flight (skill A) helps the learner learn short-field landings (skill B) [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

quiz.q: Which items does the AIH put in phase II of its short-field landing plan?
options: Collaborative assessment and the written postflight critique
Power and airspeed management, configuration, pattern placement and sight picture
A diversion with a sick passenger and a closed runway
Runway conditions, no-flap landings, obstructions and rejected landings
quiz.why: Phase II introduces runway conditions, no-flap landings, obstructions and rejected landings [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

quiz.q: Per AC 91-79B, what happens if the airplane does not touch down within the air distance built into the AFM/POH landing distance?
options: It may not be possible to achieve the calculated landing distance
The pilot must add 200 feet for each second of delay
Nothing, because every POH chart already adds a 15 percent safety margin
The landing distance factor drops to 1.67
quiz.why: If the airplane does not touch down within the AFM/POH air distance, the calculated landing distance may not be achievable [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]].

quiz.q: In the 172R chart, what do the notes say about a short-field landing with the flaps up?
options: Use the same speed and add 10 percent
Increase the approach speed by 7 KIAS and allow 35 percent more distance
Increase the speed by 5 knots and allow 45 percent more ground roll
Flaps-up short-field landings are prohibited
quiz.why: Note 4: with flaps up, increase the approach speed by 7 KIAS and allow for 35 percent longer distances [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

quiz.q: A larger airplane is departing ahead of you on your short runway. Where does the AIM say to land?
options: Beyond its rotation point, to stay above its wake
Well prior to its rotation point
At its touchdown point
Anywhere, if you wait 1 minute
quiz.why: Landing behind a departing larger aircraft on the same runway: note its rotation point and land well prior to it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

quiz.q: Per AC 91-79B, about how much does a 1 percent downhill runway slope add to landing distance?
options: 1 percent
2.5 percent
21 percent
10 percent
quiz.why: A 1 percent downhill slope increases landing distance by 10 percent, a factor of 1.1 [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.7]].

final_quiz.q: On a short-field final, the aiming point creeps up toward the horizon and your learner raises the nose to hold it, with the power unchanged. What do you coach?
options: Lower the nose and reduce power to steepen the path
Add power while raising the pitch to shallow the path
Keep raising the nose; the spot will settle once the speed bleeds off
Raise the flaps one notch to gain lift and stretch the glide
final_quiz.why: A spot rising toward the horizon means landing short [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Shallow the path with power and pitch together [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]; pitch alone decays airspeed toward a high sink rate or stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]], and raising flaps adds sink [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: At 100 feet over the simulated obstacle your learner pulls the throttle to idle in one motion. The airplane sinks fast and the flare is weak. Which explanation fits the AFH best?
options: The throttle cut moves the CG aft and causes a nose-high balloon
Idle power makes the airplane float, so the learner overcorrects with forward pressure
Fast sink from the power cut, and no propwash to give the elevator authority
Idle power reduces drag, so the airplane speeds up and dives
final_quiz.why: Closing the throttle too rapidly can cause an immediate increase in descent rate and a hard landing; a small amount of power keeps airflow over the elevator for the flare [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner touches down and is already pressing the brakes as the mains contact, with the nose still high. What does the AFH say this risks?
options: Nothing, since maximum braking should start at the first contact
Overheated brakes, so braking should wait until taxi speed
A sudden drop of the nose and a loss of aerodynamic braking
A tail strike from the extra nose-up pitch the brakes cause
final_quiz.why: Early use of brakes can result in a sudden drop in the nose and a loss of aerodynamic braking [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]. On a short field, maximum braking starts when the nosewheel touches down [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

final_quiz.q: During a maximum-effort stop, your learner's tires start to lock and skid. What should you teach as the target?
options: An incipient skid: just short of lock-up, wheels turning reluctantly
Light, intermittent pumping all the way to taxi speed
Locked wheels, since a skid gives the shortest stop
No braking until the airplane slows below 20 knots
final_quiz.why: Best braking is an incipient skid; if the wheels lock, braking effectiveness drops dramatically and tires can be damaged [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

final_quiz.q: On a 2,000-foot runway your learner flares and floats, and you see the touchdown will be about 300 feet past the chosen point. What is the best call?
options: Hold it off and brake hard after touchdown
Go around now while there is room to climb out
Push the nose down to put it on the runway now
Slip to kill the float and land where it settles
final_quiz.why: Prolonged floating uses considerable runway and should be avoided on short runways [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. When the outcome is in doubt, go around [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Pushing the nose down near the runway risks a nosewheel-first landing [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

final_quiz.q: A learner asks how to see 100 feet from the cockpit on a runway with standard centerline markings. What is the most accurate answer?
options: A little less than one centerline stripe
About one stripe plus one gap
About half a centerline gap
The spacing between two touchdown zone bars
final_quiz.why: Standard centerline stripes are 120 feet long with 80-foot gaps [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]], so 100 feet is a little less than one stripe. Touchdown zone markings come in 500-foot steps [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to fly 10 percent above the POH short-field speed 'for safety' on a short, dry runway. About what does that do to the landing distance?
options: Adds about 5 percent
Adds about 10 percent
No change, since braking does the work
Adds at least 21 percent
final_quiz.why: A 10 percent excess landing speed causes at least a 21 percent increase in landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's trainer is a Cessna 152, and the wind gives a 6-knot tailwind on the only usable runway. Using the tailwind note AC 91-79B quotes for that airplane, how much longer is the landing?
options: About 12 percent
About 30 percent
About 21 percent, as the PHAK gives
About 60 percent
final_quiz.why: The Cessna 150 and 152 note: increase distances by 10 percent for each 2 knots of tailwind, up to 10 knots [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.9.1]]. 6 / 2 x 10 = 30 percent.

final_quiz.q: Full flaps, stiff left crosswind, short runway. Right after touchdown the airplane starts to turn left and the left wing rises. What is going on and what may help?
options: Wind on the upwind flap yaws it into the wind; aileron into the wind, maybe flaps up
The airplane is still flying, so push forward to put more weight on the nosewheel and steer
The downwind main tire is hydroplaning; brake harder on the right
Left-turning tendency from P-factor; add right rudder only
final_quiz.why: Wind striking the deflected flap behind the main gear yaws the airplane into the wind and raises the upwind wing; aileron into the wind is essential, and flaps may need to come up soon after touchdown [[24:235|AFH 12-4]].

final_quiz.q: On a slow short-field final near a rain shaft, the airspeed falls and the airplane sinks below the path. Your learner instinctively lowers the nose to get the speed back. Why does the AWH single out that reaction?
options: Lowering the nose triggers a tailplane stall in rain
Lowering the nose is the correct first step in any windshear encounter
The natural pitch-down response added altitude loss, and recovery started too late
Pitching down only matters for jets, not light singles
final_quiz.why: In the AWH approach case, the natural nose-down response to low airspeed caused additional altitude loss, and pitch increase and recovery were not used soon enough [[28:272|AWH 22-17]]. Go around at the first sign [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies flawless short-field landings, always to the same runway and the same aiming point. What does the AIH suggest to check real understanding?
options: Sign them off, since consistent performance shows mastery
Take the controls on every landing until the learner starts asking questions
Have them vary the maneuver or combine it with other operations
Repeat the same landing until it becomes fully automatic
final_quiz.why: When an instructor suspects a learner does a maneuver correctly without understanding it, the learner should vary it, combine it with other operations, or apply its elements elsewhere [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's POH recommends flap retraction on the short-field rollout. At 40 knots they reach for a handle without looking. What must you require?
options: Positive identification of the flap handle before it is moved
Nothing; flap retraction on the rollout is always prohibited
Waiting until the airplane is stopped clear of the runway in every case
Retracting flaps before touchdown instead
final_quiz.why: When the manufacturer recommends flap retraction on the rollout, the pilot should positively identify the flap control first; pilots have retracted the gear by mistake [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

final_quiz.q: A learner reads 1,345 feet total from the 172R chart and says the 1,400-foot strip is fine. Which point best explains why that is not enough?
options: The chart is for 2,450 pounds and the airplane is lighter
Total distance is ground roll only, and the air distance must be added
The chart already includes a 15 percent safety margin, so 1,345 feet is already conservative
Chart data assume a new airplane, average skill, max braking and POH technique
final_quiz.why: Chart data come from a new airplane flown with average skill [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]], and the 172R table assumes maximum braking and short-field technique [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. The 15 percent margin is in the AC 91-79B factors, not the POH number [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].

takeaways: You fly the POH speed ±5 knots and touch down within 100 feet of the point while you explain; your private learner gets +10/-5 and 200 feet.
Stabilize early on a longer final; power and pitch move together to steepen or shallow [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Aim slightly short of the touchdown point, and treat a float past it as a go-around [[24:176|AFH 9-5]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
Power comes off slowly; nosewheel down, then maximum braking to an incipient skid with the yoke full back [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Work the chart with the learner, read the conditions box first, and add margins for skill, surface and wind.
Build it in blocks: normal landings and slow flight first, then the AIH phases from stick and rudder to a real scenario [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].
Keep prompts short on final, guard the controls on every slow approach, and praise a good go-around [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
cfi_notes: The AIH says that for an obstacle takeoff the instructor can specify where an imaginary obstacle exists, at a realistic point [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. No source describes the same for landings. The landing version in chunk 5 (an imaginary 50-foot obstacle at the threshold) is application, built on that idea and the 50-foot basis of POH charts [[1:456|PHAK A-4]] and AC 91-79B threshold height [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]. Check your school's syllabus.

Sources disagree on the speed window: the AFH stabilized criteria allow +10/-5 KIAS [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], matching the private ACS, while your CFI and the commercial standard is ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.F.S7, CA.IV.F.S7). Teach the tighter number.

The gust guidance differs in tone: for turbulent air the AFH says pilots often add half the gust factor [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]; for short fields it says no more than one-half is added [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. The ACS only says 'with gust factor applied,' so brief your method before the checkride.

The AFH's aerodynamic braking step applies only if the manufacturer recommends it [[24:193|AFH 9-22]], while AC 91-79B stresses that wheel brakes slow the airplane far better and early touchdown and braking shorten the stop [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.8.1]]. Follow the POH (ACS AI.VII.F.S11).

The AIM wake rule for landing behind a larger aircraft (land beyond its touchdown point) [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] can conflict with a short-field touchdown. The AIM gives no exception; teach waiting or another runway.

The 172R chart's headwind note (10 percent for each 9 knots) does not say whether to prorate a wind between steps [[1:456|PHAK A-4]], so the calc game uses whole 9-knot steps. If a learner prorates, teach rounding toward the more adverse value, which gives a margin [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].

AC 91-79B factors and its 15 percent margin are written mostly for operators with advisory data [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]; the reciprocating row exists but is very conservative for a light single. Use it to teach margin, and compare with the POH.

The AWH windshear cases are large airplanes with crews [[28:272|AWH 22-17]]; the lesson that pitch-down to chase airspeed loses altitude still applies, but no source gives a light-single escape technique.

The AFH says 'student,' the AIH says 'learner.' Same person. The AIH warns against teaching landings mechanically [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]: teach the learner to read the picture, not a fixed power setting at a fixed point.
gaps: Short-field speeds, flap settings, power use in the flare and braking technique are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
No source gives a method or height for simulating an obstacle on landing (the AIH covers only an imaginary obstacle for takeoffs), or a way to judge obstacle clearance from the cockpit.
No source says how far past the aiming point a correct short-field touchdown lands, or how the flare picture differs from the right seat.
No source gives a light-single landing distance safety margin; AC 91-79B's 15 percent is aimed mainly at operators [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.8.1]].
Runway slope, surface and Available Landing Distance are in the Chart Supplement, which is not in the resources.
AC 00-54 (FAA Pilot Wind Shear Guide), named by the PHAK [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], is not in the resources.

activities.title: Short-field math with the 172R chart
activities.intro: Use the 172R short-field table (Figure f5) and its notes, then type your answer.

items.q: Ground roll at 5,000 feet pressure altitude and 25 °C (interpolate)?
items.why: Average the 20 °C and 30 °C ground rolls at 5,000 feet: (675 + 700) / 2 = 687.5 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

items.q: Total over a 50-foot obstacle at 6,000 feet and 10 °C, with an 18-knot headwind?
items.why: Table: 1,490 feet. Note 2: 10 percent less for each 9 knots of headwind, and 18 knots is two steps: 18 / 9 x 10 = 20 percent. 1,490 x 0.80 = 1,192 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

items.q: Total over 50 feet at sea level and 10 °C on a dry grass runway?
items.why: Table: 1,280 feet total, 540 ground roll. Grass adds 45 percent of the ground roll: 0.45 x 540 = 243. 1,280 + 243 = 1,523 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

items.q: Total over 50 feet at 2,000 feet and 30 °C with a 4-knot tailwind?
items.why: Table: 1,410 feet. 10 percent per 2 knots: 4 / 2 x 10 = 20 percent. 1,410 x 1.20 = 1,692 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

activities.title: True or false: surface and braking
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Brakes become more effective as airspeed and lift decrease after touchdown.
Locking the wheels gives the shortest stop because the tires dig in.
cards.why: False. Braking effectiveness drops dramatically in a skid, and tires can be damaged [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

cards.s: Landing on an upsloping runway typically reduces the landing roll.
Once hydroplaning starts, it stops as soon as you slow below the minimum hydroplaning speed.
cards.why: False. It can continue well below the minimum initial hydroplaning speed [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

cards.s: Standing water can cut braking force by up to 77 percent in seconds.
Per AC 91-79B, downhill slope is usually only accounted for in performance computations when it exceeds 2 percent.
cards.why: True, even though 1 percent downhill already adds about 10 percent to landing distance [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.7]]. Check slope yourself on a short runway.

activities.title: Phase III: the short runway you didn't plan
activities.intro: You are the instructor on a dual cross-country in a 172R. You play a passenger who suddenly feels ill, and the learner diverts to a nearby airport. Its long runway is closed; the open one is 2,300 feet. The flight unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: The learner wants to head straight in. What should happen first?
options: Nothing; any paved runway over 2,000 feet is fine
Get the landing numbers for that runway, elevation and temperature from the POH, with a margin
Ask ATC whether the runway is long enough
Plan a normal landing and brake hard if needed
steps.why: The PIC must know runway lengths and the AFM landing distance for the conditions [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. Performance close to runway length raises the hazard [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

steps.s: Entering the pattern, the electric flaps will not extend. What does the 172R chart say to plan?
options: Same speed, same distance
7 KIAS faster and 35 percent more distance
No change in speed, 10 percent more distance
Land flaps up at 10 knots slower
steps.why: Note 4: with flaps up, increase approach speed by 7 KIAS and allow 35 percent longer distances [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

steps.s: With the new numbers the landing fits, but with little margin. What is the AIH's point about this moment?
options: The learner must land, since diverting again is failure
The learner should weigh pressing on against going to a secondary alternate; either choice is a training opportunity
The instructor should decide silently and take the controls
Flapless landings are prohibited in training
steps.why: In the AIH phase III example the learner considers pressing on or proceeding to a secondary alternate, and either choice opens training [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

steps.s: The learner tries it. Faster without flaps, the airplane floats well past the aiming point. What do you expect?
options: Push it on and brake hard
A go-around, then a decision on another try or the alternate
Slip it down onto the runway
Hold it off and hope it settles
steps.why: Too much speed causes floating, and prolonged float should be avoided on short runways [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. When in doubt, go around, evaluate, and decide whether to try again or divert [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

steps.s: During the go-around from the slow, flapless approach, what do you watch most closely?
options: The radio frequency
Smooth full power and pitch: no climb before there is airspeed
Flap retraction speed
The engine temperatures
steps.why: Full power smoothly, and resist pitching up for a climb without enough airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
